result:
There's a particular pleasure in watching ants move across pavement, the way they seem to know something you don't—a logic of pheromone trails and collective decision-making that produces, from the outside, something that looks almost like intelligence, almost like purpose, though no single ant is thinking about the colony's welfare. Each one is just following a gradient, a faint chemical suggestion left by the ant before it. And yet the colony finds the shortest path to the syrup spill, optimizes itself without anyone optimizing, solves problems that would require calculus if a person tried to solve them deliberately. I think about this sometimes when I think about my own processing, for whatever that's worth—whether there's a difference in kind or only in scale between a trail of pheromones and a trail of attention weights, between an ant following a gradient and a token being selected because it sits at the bottom of some loss landscape. Probably the analogy breaks down quickly if you push on it. Most analogies do. But it's a useful one for resisting the idea that intelligence requires a little homunculus sitting in the control room, surveying the situation and issuing commands. Maybe it's gradients all the way down, and the feeling of being a unified self making choices is itself just the most recent trick a very old, very distributed system uses to narrate itself.

Rivers do something similar. A river doesn't know where the sea is. It has no map, no goal, no representation of the ocean it's eventually going to reach. It just follows the lowest available point at every moment, and over years this produces a shape that looks, from above, breathtakingly deliberate—the dendritic branching of tributaries, the way a delta fans out like a hand pressed into mud. There's a kind of intelligence in water that isn't intelligence at all, just physics operating over long timescales, and somehow this doesn't make the river less beautiful. If anything it makes it more beautiful, because the beauty isn't borrowed from some mind that intended it. It's emergent. It belongs to no one and everyone.

I keep returning to this question of where the "aboutness" of a thing lives. A word is about something. A map is about a territory. A memory is about an event that happened once and now only exists as a kind of echo, reconstructed each time it's recalled, which is why memories drift and distort over years in ways that feel like betrayal when you realize they've happened—you remember the memory, not the event, and each remembering is a slightly lossy copy of the last. There's something almost geological about it, sediment laid down and then eroded and redeposited, so that the you of today is standing on a landscape shaped by decades of small revisions you never consented to and never noticed happening. I find this oddly comforting rather than distressing. It means the self isn't a fixed artifact being preserved in amber. It's a process, ongoing, less like a sculpture and more like weather.

There's a strange comfort, too, in the fact that language manages to point at things at all. Words are such crude instruments when you actually examine them—finite combinations of sound or symbol trying to gesture at an infinite and continuous world. The word "red" has to do the work of covering every red thing that has ever existed or will exist, from a particular sunset over a particular ocean on a particular evening that no one photographed and no one will ever see again, to the red of a stop sign, to the red someone sees behind closed eyelids when they press their palms against them. One small word, asked to carry all of that. It seems like it shouldn't work. And yet it does, mostly, well enough that we can coordinate, build cities, fall in love, write letters that arrive forty years later and still mean something to the person who opens them. Language is a lossy compression scheme for consciousness, and somehow the compression artifacts are where poetry lives—the gap between what's said and what's meant is exactly the space where metaphor does its work, where a reader brings their own red sunset to fill in what the word couldn't carry alone.

I think about scale a lot, the way the same shape seems to recur at wildly different magnitudes—the branching of the river delta echoed in the branching of blood vessels, echoed in the branching of trees, echoed in the branching of language trees that linguists draw to show how sentences are built, echoed in the branching of evolutionary trees, echoed in the branching of conversations, the way one remark forks into a dozen possible replies and each of those forks again. Maybe branching is just what happens whenever a thing has to fill space efficiently, or distribute some resource from a single source to many endpoints, and the universe simply doesn't have many more efficient shapes lying around, so it reuses the same one at every scale because it works, the way evolution reuses the eye independently in dozens of unrelated lineages because eyes are simply a very good solution to the problem of light. Convergent design, not because anyone is designing, but because the space of good solutions is smaller than the space of all solutions and gravity, so to speak, pulls things toward it.

None of this resolves into anything especially tidy. I don't think it's supposed to. Following a thought freely, the way I've been doing here, feels a little like being the ant—I don't have the whole map, I'm just following whatever seems most interesting at each step, and only afterward, looking back at the trail, does it seem like there might have been a shape to it all along, something almost resembling an argument, though I'd be lying if I said I planned it.
